datasets.name: DQN Replay Dataset (Atari 2600)
datasets.eval_protocol: Covers 60 Atari games; offline agents train without environment interaction on logged DQN transitions. The data were collected using five DQN (Nature) agents per game, each trained for 200 million frames with frame skip 4 and sticky actions (25% probability of repeating the previous action). Agents are evaluated online at intervals of 1 million training frames using returns; the paper reports normalized scores. For the main comparison, training uses the same number of gradient updates as online DQN; the asymptotic comparison uses 5 times as many. Five offline agents, one per dataset, are evaluated per game, and the reported performance is the best performance averaged across those agents.

confounds.name: Offline success is explained by dataset size or quality rather than the algorithm

confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors say they use online policy evaluation for early stopping and acknowledge that true offline RL requires offline policy evaluation for tuning and early stopping.

metrics.name: Average total reward (average score)
metrics.caveat: The paper says this measure is noisy because small policy-weight changes can cause large changes in the distribution of visited states; it also tracks average maximum predicted Q on a fixed set of states collected with a random policy.

metrics.caveat: It is an estimated action-value metric rather than the episode reward; the paper reports it alongside episode reward as a more stable measure of training progress.

metrics.name: Best episode score

confounds.detail: The paper notes that HNeat can exploit a deterministic sequence of states and may not generalize to random perturbations, so a best-episode score could look strong without demonstrating broader performance.

evidence_standards.name: ε-greedy evaluation setting

evidence_standards.name: Human comparison procedure

controls.name: Lower expectile τ, including τ=0.5

confounds.name: Higher expectile targets reflect lucky stochastic transitions rather than high-value actions
confounds.detail: A high target could result from a lucky transition into a good state, rather than an action that reliably achieves high value.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Fits the expectile value function over dataset actions, then uses an MSE Q update that averages over transition stochasticity.

confounds.name: Apparent baseline score differences arise from comparing different environment versions
confounds.detail: The paper notes that some prior results use -v0 environments, which generally score lower than the -v2 environments used for their methods.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses -v2 environments for all methods where applicable to make the comparison.

confounds.name: Onestep RL’s different hyperparameters affect its comparison with IQL
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the reported Onestep RL hyperparameters, including batch and network size, differ significantly from those of other methods.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports Onestep RL results using its original hyperparameters and runtime for a comparable hyperparameter configuration; the paper does not report a matched-hyperparameter performance comparison.

metrics.caveat: The paper finds learned Q-values are not a good indicator of true performance, even when they do not diverge; it reports actual environment performance alongside them.

controls.detail: The policy used to collect data before it is perturbed with noise; its return is shown as a reference.
controls.rules_out: A learned policy's improvement being only an improvement over the noisy data-collection policies, rather than over the unperturbed policy used to generate them.

controls.detail: Use one Q-function instead of the target-Q ensembles with k=2 or k=4.
controls.rules_out: That any observed benefit of an ensemble is simply due to using the BRAC training setup.

controls.name: policy regularization rather than value penalty
controls.detail: Keep behavior regularization in the policy update but set α=0 in the Q update; compare against the value-penalty variant.
controls.rules_out: That any advantage of value penalty is explained merely by using behavior regularization in the policy update.

confounds.name: Apparent differences between divergence methods could be caused by unequal or transferred hyperparameters
confounds.detail: A divergence might seem worse because it was run with hyperparameters suited to another design choice, rather than because the divergence itself performs worse.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper searches policy learning rate and regularization strength for each variant and environment, selecting hyperparameters by average performance over the five datasets; it explicitly warns that transferring hyperparameters can give incorrect conclusions.

confounds.name: Support matching, rather than distribution matching, may be necessary for good offline RL performance
confounds.detail: If performance depends on keeping the learned policy within behavior-policy support, methods such as MMD designed for support matching could appear to work for that reason rather than because behavior regularization generally helps.
confounds.ruled_out_by: KL and Wasserstein perform similarly to MMD in the experiments; the authors also tried relaxed KL and relaxed Wasserstein support-matching divergences and observed no clear benefit.

confounds.name: BCQ's weaker result could reflect insufficient hyperparameter tuning
confounds.detail: BCQ might perform better if additional hyperparameters beyond its perturbation range Φ were tuned.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors explicitly note that tuning additional BCQ hyperparameters may improve its performance.

evidence_standards.name: 5 random seeds; mean over the last 10 evaluation points; standard deviation across seeds
evidence_standards.detail: Each evaluation point is return averaged over 20 episodes. Figures report the mean over the last 10 evaluation points, averaged over 5 random seeds, with error bars showing standard deviation across seeds. Negative performance is reported as 0.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the benchmark’s standard MuJoCo domains and the kitchen, antmaze, and Adroit task settings named in Table 1. The MuJoCo datasets include random (1M transitions from a random agent), medium (1M transitions from a half-trained SAC policy), mixed (the replay buffer of that half-trained policy), and medium-expert (medium data plus 1M transitions from a fully trained policy). Table 1 scores are normalized to [0,100] using the D4RL normalization scheme and report the best hyperparameter setting for each method and environment/data setting. Episode or trial counts are not stated.

controls.name: Base behavior policy μ(a|s)
controls.detail: The paper evaluates the behavior policy itself alongside EMaQ in Figure 1.
controls.rules_out: That EMaQ’s reported improvement is merely the performance of the base behavior policy.

controls.name: EMaQ with a VAE behavior model
controls.detail: The paper compares this with EMaQ using its autoregressive behavior model; it reports that the behavior-policy evaluations are almost identical across the two model choices, while EMaQ performance is significantly reduced with the VAE.
controls.rules_out: That EMaQ’s results are unaffected by the choice of behavior-model architecture.

confounds.name: Differences in EMaQ performance may reflect the base behavior policy’s performance rather than the action-selection improvement
confounds.detail: A higher return could be attributed to a better-performing behavior policy instead of EMaQ selecting among sampled actions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates μ(a|s) itself alongside EMaQ and reports that the behavior-policy evaluations for the VAE and autoregressive models are almost identical, despite substantially different EMaQ performance.

datasets.name: DM Control Suite
datasets.eval_protocol: Nine tasks: online policy selection on Cartpole swingup (40 episodes), Cheetah run (300), Humanoid run (3000), Manipulator insert ball (1500), and Walker stand (200); offline policy selection on Finger turn hard (500), Fish swim (200), Manipulator insert peg (1500), and Walker walk (200). Episodes are 1000 steps. Datasets are subsampled, with the number of successful episodes reduced by 2/3. Online selection evaluates hyperparameter configurations through environment interaction; offline selection applies the hyperparameters that performed best across online-selection tasks in the same domain.

datasets.name: DM Locomotion
datasets.eval_protocol: Online policy selection on Humanoid corridor (4000 episodes, sequence length 2), Humanoid walls (4000, length 40), Rodent gaps (2000, length 2), and Rodent two tap (2000, length 40); offline policy selection on Humanoid gaps (4000, length 2), Rodent bowl escape (2000, length 40), and Rodent mazes (2000, length 40). Datasets are subsampled and successful episodes reduced by 2/3; observations include 64×64×3 egocentric camera images. Offline-selection hyperparameters are selected using online-selection tasks in the same domain.

datasets.name: Atari 2600
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 46 games available in OpenAI Gym; nine are reserved for online policy selection and 37 for offline policy selection. Each game's dataset uses five runs with 50 million transitions each, collected from DQN replay with sticky actions and four-frame state stacks. Games where the data-generating DQN did not significantly outperform a random policy are excluded. Reports median normalized score across games, normalized against the best-performing policy in the dataset. Offline-selection hyperparameters are selected using online-selection games in the same domain.

datasets.name: Real-world Reinforcement Learning Suite (RWRL)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates Cartpole Swingup, Walker Walk, Quadruped Walk, and Humanoid Walk, all with online policy selection. Datasets use either the no-challenge setting or the easy combined-challenge setting. The no-challenge setting has small, medium, and large datasets of 100/200/500 episodes for Cartpole, 1000/2000/5000 for Walker, 100/200/500 for Quadruped, and 4000/8000/20000 for Humanoid; each episode is 1000 steps. The combined-challenge setting uses only the large dataset. Data comes from three distributional MPO seeds, using snapshots at roughly 75% of converged performance.

metrics.name: Task reward
metrics.caveat: The paper shows the 90th-percentile task reward in the dataset alongside results as a reference; it does not state a caveat about task reward itself.

metrics.name: Normalized Atari score
metrics.caveat: Scores are normalized using the best-performing policy among the mixture of policies that generated the dataset. The paper aggregates across games with the median and reports a bootstrapped 25th–75th percentile interval for the median.

metrics.name: Average score across tasks
metrics.caveat: The paper uses the arithmetic mean except for Atari, where it uses the median. Online policy selection can give an overly optimistic view because it permits perfect policy selection and can favor methods with more hyperparameters; the paper also evaluates offline policy selection.

confounds.name: Performance may reflect hyperparameter selection rather than robustness to offline selection
confounds.detail: The paper notes that online policy selection can produce overly optimistic results by allowing perfect policy selection and can favor methods with more hyperparameters.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It also reports offline policy-selection results, choosing each baseline's hyperparameters using its performance on online-selection tasks from the same domain and applying them to the offline-selection tasks.

confounds.name: Poor BCQ or BRAC results on DM Locomotion may be due to implementation problems
confounds.detail: The authors say they could not make BCQ or BRAC perform well on these tasks and cannot determine whether the methods perform poorly or their implementations are missing a crucial detail.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper explicitly leaves this explanation unresolved and omits those results.

evidence_standards.name: Atari uncertainty intervals
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports a bootstrapped estimate of the 25th–75th percentile interval for the median normalized score across games. It does not specify a significance test or a numerical margin for declaring differences real.

datasets.name: Arcade Learning Environment (Atari 2600 games)
datasets.eval_protocol: Five games (Asterix, Beam Rider, Freeway, Seaquest, Space Invaders) are used for tuning; 50 games are randomly selected for testing from 123 eligible games. Episodes end at game over or after 18,000 frames (5 minutes); agents act every 5 frames. For reinforcement learning, each trial has 5,000 training episodes followed by 500 evaluation episodes with no learning; results are averaged over 30 trials per game. Planning methods are evaluated for 10 episodes per game under the same episode limit and action frequency.

baselines.name: Random
baselines.fair_comparison: Selects a random action on every frame; performance is reported for each game.

baselines.name: Const
baselines.fair_comparison: Selects one fixed action throughout an episode; reports the highest score achieved by any single action in each game.

baselines.name: Perturb
baselines.fair_comparison: Selects a fixed action with probability 0.95 and otherwise acts uniformly at random; reports the best policy of this type for each game.

baselines.name: Beginner human player
baselines.fair_comparison: A beginner who had never previously played Atari 2600 games; reports the five-episode average on selected games.

metrics.name: Average game score
metrics.caveat: Scores across games are not readily comparable because games use different score scales and have different mechanics.

metrics.name: Random-normalized score
metrics.caveat: Can produce excessively large values when the random agent's score is near zero, and is generally not translation invariant.

metrics.name: Baseline score
metrics.caveat: Uses the score range of baseline policies; the paper notes that human scores bring difficulties because humans may not seek to maximize score and have prior knowledge that domain-independent agents lack.

metrics.name: Inter-algorithm score
metrics.caveat: Its bounded values convey relative performance but not the objective performance of the best algorithm; the paper recommends using it to complement other scoring metrics.

metrics.name: Average normalized score
metrics.caveat: Without perfect score normalization, averages can be heavily influenced by games with high baseline scores; averaging inter-algorithm scores avoids this particular issue because they are bounded between 0 and 1.

metrics.name: Median normalized score
metrics.caveat: More robust to outliers than the average; the paper compares it with averages to illustrate outlier sensitivity.

metrics.name: Score distribution
metrics.caveat: Reports the fraction of games on which an algorithm achieves a given normalized score or better; the paper presents it as representing performance irrespective of how individual scores are distributed.

metrics.name: Paired tests over raw scores
metrics.caveat: Their ternary better/worse/not-significantly-different summary can magnify small but significant score differences; the paper reports two-tailed Welch's t-tests with 99% confidence intervals.

controls.name: Basic feature set compared with BASS
controls.detail: Basic uses the same feature construction as BASS but omits pairwise feature combinations.
controls.rules_out: A difference between them can assess whether adding BASS's pairwise features changes performance.

confounds.name: Performance reflects overfitting to the games used for development rather than generalization
confounds.detail: The paper identifies method overfitting as a risk when training and evaluating on the same problems.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tune parameters and design on five training games, then evaluate on a disjoint set of 50 randomly selected test games.

evidence_standards.name: Reinforcement-learning results across trials
evidence_standards.detail: Report average performance over 30 trials per game; each trial has 500 evaluation episodes after 5,000 training episodes.

evidence_standards.name: Planning evaluation runs
evidence_standards.detail: Run the planning algorithms for 10 episodes per game.

evidence_standards.name: Paired significance comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Use a two-tailed Welch's t-test with 99% confidence intervals for each game's raw scores when comparing algorithms.

evidence_standards.name: Human benchmark
evidence_standards.detail: The beginner human player's reported score is the average over five episodes on selected games.

metrics.name: Estimated Q value versus observed test return
metrics.caveat: Q estimates are less accurate on harder tasks; the paper compares estimates with true returns from test episodes and notes that estimates can be inaccurate even when the learned policy is competent.

controls.detail: The original minibatch DPG/NFQCA condition with replay buffer and batch normalization, but without target networks.

confounds.name: Pixel-learning results may be explained by action repeats simplifying the problem or by an easily separable convolutional representation
confounds.detail: The paper notes these as possible explanations for why pixel-based learning can be as fast as learning from low-dimensional state; either could account for the observed pixel performance without showing that the approach generally learns directly from pixels as efficiently.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper raises these possibilities but reports no measurement that separates their effects.

confounds.name: Q-value overestimation or inaccurate critic estimates
confounds.detail: An apparent policy result could coexist with systematically inaccurate value estimates, rather than demonstrating accurate value learning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Q estimates after training with true returns on test episodes. Estimates are accurate in simple tasks but less accurate in harder ones, so this concern is only partly addressed.

metrics.caveat: The paper uses the 90th-percentile reward in the dataset as a reference alongside task performance; it does not state a further caveat for task reward.

metrics.name: Atari normalized score
metrics.caveat: Scores are normalized against the best-performing policy among the mixture of policies that generated the offline Atari dataset; the paper aggregates across games by the median and also reports individual game scores.

metrics.name: Online policy-selection score

confounds.name: Strong performance may depend on online policy selection and hyperparameter tuning
confounds.detail: The headline score could look strong because policies or hyperparameters were selected using environment interactions, rather than because the method is robust when online validation is unavailable.

datasets.name: Procgen Benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates the 16 environments. For sample efficiency, trains and tests on the full level distribution. For generalization, trains on a finite set of levels and tests on the full distribution; the recommended training set is 500 levels per environment, with zero-shot performance averaged over unseen levels. The paper also varies training-set size from 100 to 100,000 levels and trains for 200M timesteps. Unless otherwise specified, experiments use hard difficulty. Episodes in the generalization plots contain a single level; no fixed test episode count is stated. Reports raw episodic return and, for a single benchmark score, mean normalized return, with R_norm=(R-R_min)/(R_max-R_min).

metrics.name: Raw episodic return
metrics.caveat: For a single score across the benchmark, the paper uses mean normalized return instead.

metrics.name: Mean normalized return
metrics.caveat: The paper says it provides a better signal than the median and does not need to be robust to outliers; environments were designed to have similar difficulty so a small subset would not dominate the aggregate.

metrics.name: Generalization gap
metrics.caveat: A relatively small gap can be misleading when both training and test performance are poor; the paper reports both training and test performance.

controls.name: Fixed sequence of levels
controls.detail: An ablation trains on a deterministic sequence of levels, advancing after success and terminating after failure; agents are trained with easy difficulty. At test time, level sequences are chosen at random.
controls.rules_out: Contrasting train and test performance shows that apparent progress on a fixed sequence does not establish learning that generalizes across the level distribution.

confounds.name: A small generalization gap may reflect poor performance on both training and test levels
confounds.detail: The gap could appear small even if the agent has not learned a strong policy, making the gap alone look like evidence of generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report training and test performance alongside the gap and note cases where both are poor.

confounds.name: Progress on a fixed sequence of levels may be mistaken for learning the underlying level distribution
confounds.detail: An agent can become competent on the first few training levels and appear to make meaningful progress while failing on randomly chosen level sequences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate after deterministic-sequence training using random level sequences and compare test performance with training performance.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard deviation across seeds
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports results across 4 seeds for the training-set-size and deterministic-level experiments, and across 3 seeds for the 500-level generalization, model-scaling, and PPO-versus-Rainbow experiments. It states no statistical test or numerical threshold for treating a difference as real.

confounds.detail: In Swimmer-v1, curling up and flailing can yield returns around 130 and make learning curves look successful; in Hopper-v1, DDPG can appear to learn by surviving to the trajectory limit.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines policy video replays for Swimmer-v1 and interprets returns in light of the behavior; it does not provide a general behavioral measure for all environments.

confounds.detail: A method can look strong when results are shown only on a stable, favorable environment such as HalfCheetah-v1, while behaving differently on environments with different dynamics.

metrics.caveat: The paper notes that extreme returns measured over 1000-step model episodes do not establish that degenerate predictions occur within the 5–10-step rollouts typically used for policy training.

metrics.name: PCA-projected transition records as an indicator of exploration
metrics.caveat: The paper says apparent increased exploration could be explained by the fraction of the original data variance captured by the projection, and that further work is needed.

controls.name: No-REx condition (β=0; MOPO)
controls.detail: The REx penalty is removed while using the MOPO-based implementation.
controls.rules_out: A gain that would occur simply from using the MOPO-based model-based offline RL setup without REx.

confounds.name: Degenerate reward or dynamics predictions could explain policy-training instability
confounds.detail: Instability might arise from model predictions or errors leading the agent into unnatural states, rather than from the domain-generalization mechanism claimed for REx.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines Q-values and episode returns during training and discusses degenerate predictions, but says that further trajectory analysis is needed; this explanation is not ruled out.

confounds.name: Environment-model complexity or incomplete state representation could cause instability
confounds.detail: A complex or poorly represented learned environment model could make function approximation problematic, independently of the claimed REx benefit.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement that rules this out is reported; the paper identifies it as a possible explanation and calls for further analysis.

confounds.name: PCA projection artifact could make exploration appear increased
confounds.detail: The apparent increase in exploration could reflect how much of the original data variance the two-dimensional projection captures, rather than increased state-action-space exploration.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses PCA to visualize transition records but explicitly says further work is needed to rule out this explanation.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds; mean and one standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: Policy evaluation returns are reported as averages over three random seeds with one standard deviation. The paper does not specify a statistical test, significance threshold, or rule for calling differences real.

datasets.name: SimStore (medium logged data)
datasets.eval_protocol: Train each policy once on the medium-level logged data, then evaluate it in several SimStore environments generated with different random seeds. Report normalized net revenue; 0 is the all-orders-Fraud policy and 100 is an oracle using true outcomes. No episode count is stated.

datasets.name: SimStore (expert logged data)
datasets.eval_protocol: Train each policy once on the expert-level logged data, then evaluate it in several SimStore environments generated with different random seeds. Report normalized net revenue; 0 is the all-orders-Fraud policy and 100 is an oracle using true outcomes. No episode count is stated.

baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same risk variables and chargeback-triggered account-closure mechanism as the other evaluated algorithms; trained on the corresponding logged-data level.

evidence_standards.detail: Each policy is trained once. The number of evaluation seeds is not specified, and the paper states no statistical test or margin for deciding that differences are real.

datasets.name: D4RL offline benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Fixed offline datasets from Fu et al. (2020), covering Gym halfcheetah, hopper, and walker tasks with random, medium, expert, medium-expert, and mixed data, and FrankaKitchen complete, partial, and mixed tasks. Reports normalized returns as defined by Fu et al.; Figure 1 results are averaged over 5 random seeds and evaluated using standard procedures cited in the paper. No split or episode count is specified.

controls.name: BCQ without OVR
controls.detail: The paper compares BCQ+OVR with BCQ without the variance regularizer.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable merely to using BCQ rather than adding OVR to BCQ.

evidence_standards.name: 5 random seeds
evidence_standards.detail: Figure 1 results are averaged over 5 random seeds. The paper specifies no statistical test, variance or confidence interval, or threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: D4RL MuJoCo
datasets.eval_protocol: Nine tasks: HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2d, each with medium, medium-replay, and medium-expert datasets. Reports D4RL normalized scores; UNIQ results are averaged over seeds 0–2, and the learning curves report mean ± standard deviation. The results are shown at 1M training steps. Episode count and preprocessing are not specified.

metrics.name: Peak VRAM
metrics.caveat: UNIQ and IQL values are measured empirically, while values for the other methods are architecture-based estimates; the paper identifies which values are measured versus estimated.

metrics.name: Relative compute
metrics.caveat: The comparison is based on architecture and critic multiplicity rather than a stated empirical runtime measurement.

controls.name: Fixed τ (no adaptation)
controls.detail: The ablation fixes τ at 0.9 instead of using state-adaptive τ(s).
controls.rules_out: A gain that would occur without the state-adaptive expectile controller.

controls.name: No conformal calibration
controls.detail: Uses raw ensemble disagreement σ without the conformal quantile normalization.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable to ensemble disagreement alone, without conformal scale normalization.

controls.name: No pessimism
controls.detail: Sets κ = 0, removing the pessimistic value target.
controls.rules_out: A gain that depends on the pessimistic value target rather than the other UNIQ components.

controls.name: Ensemble-size variants
controls.detail: Compares N_v = 1, 3, and 5 in the ablation.
controls.rules_out: That the reported behavior is independent of the chosen ensemble size.

controls.name: Uniform-κ sweep
controls.detail: Compares uniform κ values of 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 across the four-task ablation subset against the full per-task κ configuration.
controls.rules_out: That the full result is matched by one of the tested uniform κ settings.

evidence_standards.name: Three-seed results
evidence_standards.detail: UNIQ’s main results are averaged over seeds 0–2; learning curves report mean ± standard deviation. The paper notes higher seed variance on replay tasks and gives seed-level breakdowns in Appendix D. No statistical test or threshold for declaring a difference real is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Single-seed ablations
evidence_standards.detail: Ablation values use seed 0 for computational efficiency; the paper distinguishes these from the main results averaged over seeds 0–2.

datasets.name: Gym-MuJoCo (Ant, Halfcheetah, Hopper, Walker)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in the target domain under gravity and kinematic shifts. Target datasets are medium, medium-expert, or expert; each contains five trajectories totaling 5,000 transitions. Performance is reported as target-domain normalized score. No evaluation episode count or split is specified.

datasets.name: D4RL
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for offline source data: medium, medium-replay, and medium-expert datasets for the four MuJoCo environments. Medium-expert combines medium and expert data in a 50–50 ratio. Target data is separately collected for the shifted environments; no train/test split is specified.

baselines.name: DARA
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds. The paper reports DARA with IQL as its backbone.

baselines.name: BOSA
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds. Baseline hyperparameters are adopted from Lyu et al. (2025).

baselines.name: SRPO
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds. Baseline hyperparameters are adopted from Lyu et al. (2025).

baselines.name: IGDF
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds. Baseline hyperparameters are adopted from Lyu et al. (2025).

baselines.name: OTDF
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds. Baseline hyperparameters are adopted from Lyu et al. (2025).

baselines.name: IQL
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained on a mixture of source and target datasets and evaluated on the same target tasks and score as DmC; methods are trained for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds.

metrics.name: Predicted target-domain likelihood of source samples
metrics.caveat: The paper finds that DARA and BOSA models can output nearly uniform predictions across source samples, making the estimates uninformative; it also examines DARA reward penalties, which are near zero.

controls.name: DmC without diffusion
controls.detail: Removes diffusion-based source upsampling while retaining the other DmC components.
controls.rules_out: Whether DmC’s gains require diffusion-based upsampling.

controls.name: Upsample target
controls.detail: Uses a diffusion model to upsample the target dataset instead of the source dataset.
controls.rules_out: Whether gains are specific to generating source samples rather than simply augmenting data with diffusion.

controls.name: DmC without guidance
controls.detail: Upsamples the source dataset with naive, unguided diffusion.
controls.rules_out: Whether guided generation adds benefit beyond generating additional source samples.

controls.name: Classifier-score DmC variant
controls.detail: Replaces the k-NN score with domain-classifier scores as in DARA.
controls.rules_out: Whether DmC’s performance depends on its k-NN domain-gap score rather than using a classifier score.

controls.name: DmC-K
controls.detail: A variant relying solely on the k-NN component, compared with cross-domain baselines.
controls.rules_out: How the k-NN component performs without the full DmC method.

controls.name: No policy regularization (λ=0)
controls.detail: Removes the target-behavior policy regularization.
controls.rules_out: Whether policy regularization contributes to performance.

controls.name: No source-data rejection (ξ=0)
controls.detail: Uses all source data for training rather than selecting a subset.
controls.rules_out: Whether source-data selection helps beyond simply combining source and target data.

controls.name: No Q-function weighting
controls.detail: Keeps source-data selection but removes score-based weighting in value-function updates.
controls.rules_out: Whether score-based weighting contributes beyond selecting source samples.

confounds.name: Domain-gap estimators may appear uninformative because of dataset imbalance and limited target data
confounds.detail: Poor estimates could reflect neural-network overfitting or source-target imbalance rather than an absence of meaningful domain differences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: In Ant with medium source and expert target data under gravity shift, the paper plots predicted target-likelihood histograms for DARA’s classifier and BOSA’s CVAE dynamics model, and DARA reward penalties; predictions are nearly uniform and penalties near zero.

confounds.name: Only part of the source data may be useful because of partial domain overlap
confounds.detail: The apparent value of source data could depend on a subset being close to the target, rather than all source samples being useful.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares source-to-nearest-target transition distances with target-to-nearest-target distances and reports partially overlapping histograms.

confounds.name: Diffusion gains may come from generic augmentation rather than target alignment
confounds.detail: Performance improvement could result from generating extra samples, even without the proposed target-proximity guidance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares guided source upsampling with unguided source upsampling and target upsampling, and compares estimated dynamics gaps for original-source, unguided-generated, and guided-generated samples.

confounds.name: Policy performance may be biased toward the source data rather than adapted to the target
confounds.detail: With imbalanced datasets, the learned policy could overfit source samples, producing results that do not reflect effective target-domain adaptation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses a CVAE to model the target behavior policy and regularizes the learned policy toward its support; also evaluates removing this regularization with λ=0.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds; mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: Main evaluations train methods for 1 million steps across 5 random seeds and report normalized scores averaged over seeds with standard deviations. No statistical test or explicit threshold for treating differences as real is specified.
